KROONSTAD RUNNING DRY?

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Kroonstad may be the first Free State town to run completely dry.The town's water reservoirs are on their last capacity and the False River from which they pump water to the town, almost dry.What then

Further information:
KROONSTAD WATER SITUATION

- Kroonstad Municipality sent out a notice two weeks ago that the town would have no water for three days this week (Wednesday to Friday) because of maintanence to one pump

- The entire town is not without water, because there is still water left in the reservoir in town, but most parts of the town is without water

- There is, however, greater concern over the water situation in Kroonstad: it could be the first town in the Free State to completely run dry and it could happen very soon: two to three weeks was an estimation given at a meeting last night
- The town serves a population of about 150 000 (figure to be confirmed)

- The Sterkfontein Dam is currently empty

- The Groblersdam – that pumps water into the Bloemhof Dam – is nearly empty

- The Bloemhof Dam is Kroonstad’s reservoir Dam and is currenly standing at 0,2%

- The last dam that feeds water to Kroonstad is the Barend Wessels Dam – situated in the Vals River. Water to the town is currently being pumped to the town from this dam and it is at the lowest percentage it has ever been

- Kroonstad uses 37 million litres of water per day

- Even if ALL the boreholes in town are fully and a 100% operational, it will only provide 1 million litres of water

WANTS KROONSTAD TO BE DECLARED DISASTER AREA

- The Kroonstad Municipality is currently in a process with the Department of Water Affairs to have the town declared as a disaster area

- Only when it has been declared as a disaster area, would the National Defence Force be able to help with the drilling of extra boreholes or supplying water to residents in town if the town runs dry

- Supplying water with water tankers alone, would not be efficient to supply water to all the residents in town


CONSEQUENCES FOR BIG BUSINESSES

- Kroonstad has a few huge industries in town. These include:
- ** Sasko – not as big as it once was – but still a business that uses a lot of water
- ** Premier Milling – wheat and maize mills
- ** CC Chicken – supplies chicken countrywide and employs 600 workers – they have recently sunked 6 boreholes, but say it will still not provide them with enough water and if the town runs dry, they will have to close the business and let the workers go until there is water again
- ** Country Meat & Fernick Abbatoir – they have recently sunked 4 boreholes and they are also concerned that these 4 boreholes will not provide enough water for them to continue with their business as they currently do. They provide meat countrywide

Press Release:


Kroonstad High and Dry
The drought has already crippled many Free State towns. Now crumbling municipal infrastructure is compounding water shortages and could soon leave the province’s third largest town high and dry. With no rain forecast for the next five months and water resources dwindling rapidly, Carte Blanche asks – will Kroonstad be left with not a drop of water in coming weeks?


Script:


KROONSTAND RUNNING DRY SCRIPT

PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK

The drought has had devastating consequences on our country – ruined harvests, farmers going under, steep increases in food prices and firm water restrictions. Many smaller towns have already run dry, but now the Free State’s third largest town is facing a massive disaster.

[chopper fx]

Kroonstad’s water supply originates in the Vals River.
In full flow the river stretches between 25 to 30 metres wide. Now it’s reduced to a mere trickle – and can no longer sustain the water supply needs of Kroonstad’s almost 120-thousand residents.

DEVI LINK: Maokeng is a large township on the outskirts of Kroonstad. By Tuesday this week it was estimated that 90% of residents here haven’t had water for the past 11 days.

With no running water since the 7th of May, Christina Ncedane has had no choice but to leave her mentally disabled son at home alone - and walk with her grandchild to a nearby township to ask for water.

DEVI: Mama, how long you don’t have water here now?

CHRISTINA NCEDANE: One week and a half.

DEVI: Not one drop?

CHRISTINA NCEDANE: Nothing.

Christina uses the rain water she collected last weekend for household chores, but also has to make sure she has enough drinking water for Godfrey.

CHRISTINA: Ek het worry met daai seuntjie van my. Daai seuntjie van my, as hy nie kry die water, hy val net so. (I am concerned about that son of mine. My son – if he doesn’t get water, he falls; he just falls over.)

The Boitumela regional hospital – close to Maokeng - was also hit by water shortages as running water was intermittent throughout this week.

And Local Maokeng businessman Morena Thebe’s car wash and fast food businesses have also been impacted.

MORENA THEBE: Only God knows, but without water my car wash business is going to close.


CHRIS DALTON: At the moment they are riding in water tankers and people are standing in queues as long as you can see with five liter cans to get water to drink.

Chris Dalton is a Kroonstad resident and municipal councillor.

CHRIS DALTON: We need some serious interventions and it has to happen very quickly.

Derek Whitfield is a hydro/geologist whose company was contracted to fix the town’s nine existing municipal boreholes of which only three are operational.

DEREK WHITFIELD: Once in the surface water have been used, there is no more water supply. The only water left in Kroonstad will be groundwater.

But the water supply from the existing nine municipal boreholes will only supply one million litres a day. And it’s unknown how much water is available underground.

DEREK WHITFIELD: Kroonstad’s average daily consumption is about 35 million litres a day. There is a big shortfall.

A realistic forecast predicts that the natural water supply will be depleted in the next three weeks.

DEVI LINK: It’s only when you’re up in the air that you get a full understanding that there is no water here. Below me is the Serfontein Dam. It is virtually empty.

Kroonstad’s water supply flows from the Vals River through the first supply dam, which is Serfontein Dam. Spaski Geldenhuis is the chairperson of Kroonstad Business and Tourism.

SPASKI GELDENHUIS: All dams in Kroonstad are at a zero percent level like the one we are standing in now.

DEVI: So we are standing in the dam now?

SPASKI GELDENHUIS: This is the river bank this is supposed to be full at least. There should be people sitting here and catching fish.

From here, the water flows on towards the Globlers Dam from where water is pumped into Bloemhoek Dam.

This picture of the water level in the Bloemhoek Dam was taken less than a month ago. Since then, the water level has dropped drastically.

DEVI LINK: Bloemhoek serves as a storage dam for the city of Kroonstad. We are flying over what used to be the dam, but as you can see, there is absolutely nothing here besides a little water and flamingo’s.

THARINE HURTER: With enough water that can be pumped into our stotage dam, Bloemhoek Dam, of 26 000 megalitres capacity divided by 35 megalitres per day demand, we can have enough water for two years.

Tharine Hurter is the editor of Kroonstad’s local newspaper.

THARINE HURTER: Either the cables to the pumping station has been stolen tight under the nose of the 24-hour security company or it is not maintained or in for maintanence – it’s never ever working at 100% capacity.

The municipality has confirmed that since the cable theft, they have increased the number of security guards and currently only two of the pumps at Groblers Dam are working.
Added to this, there are serious questions surrounding the infrastructure and maintenance of the water supply systems.

CHRIS DALTON: I would say 30% of blame should be on municipality for not making adequate plans, for not maintaining the existing water systems that we got, dams boreholes. For not implementing water restrictions timeously.

The Municipal Manager, Mnce/disi Mq/wathi declined our request for an interview, saying it was “premature to talk about the matter.”
But spokesperson Khojane Madiba eventually granted us an interview.

KHOJANE MADIBA: We have put water restrictions in place. December, again, February, again May, we have now reduced the usuage of water – we are saying to people they must 15 kilolitres per month .

DEVI: Why are we in this situation?

KHOJANE MADIBA: We are in this situation Because there is no rain.

DEVI: It is not just the rain.

KHOJANE MADIBA: There is no water in the dams.

DEVI: So you are blaming you completely on the drought?

KHOJANE MADIBA: I don’t understand – are you saying we…

DEVI: I am asking you, we have this situation in Kroonstad 100% because of the drought?

KHOJANE MADIBA: Yes, it is as a result of the drought!

DEVI: This is not just as a result of the drought? You have had failing infrastructure issues, lack of maintanence for year?

KHOJANE MADIBA: The failing of infrastructure has contributed to the disaster? Is that what you are saying?

DEVI: Yes, that is what I am saying!

KHOJANE MADIBA: In any case, the problem with infrastructure in Kroonstad or in Moqhaka, we have got infrastructure that is old. And it has been there for years. People who constructed it, probably did not anticipate that the growth of the population is going to be too much.

The municipal boreholes also haven’t been maintained over the years.

DEREK WHITFIELD: The municipal boreholes that exist were drilled a long time ago for the drought in the early 90s, so their condition has deteriorated and they do need rejuvination.

But the water from the boreholes that are operational will have to be treated before being consumed.

DEREK WHITFIELD: Some of the boreholes are contaminated with e-coli, that is from sewer contamination. One of the boreholes in town is contaminated with hydro-carbon. One of the oil companies has been notified and they have taken samples.

But it seems that contaminated tap water has been an issue in the past.
Residents raised the alarm when water flowing from their taps looked like this - just three months ago.

RESIDENT: I really don’t know what to say.

The municipality said the water purification system is being upgraded to the tune of R39,2 million and will be completed in July.

THARINE HURTER: Moqhaka Municipality only budgeted R56 million in the coming bookyear 2016/2017 for repairs and maintanence. R56 million out of R670 million budget is not enough.

Residents are questioning the municipality’s lack of urgency to the water crisis. This water leaked from an open waste valve on the Suid/rand reservoir for six days this month.

KHOJANA MADIBA: We agree that the leakages somehow creates to the problem of not having the water and we have been working very hard with out dedicated employees to close those leaks. We are satisfied now with the progress we have made.

DEVI: I have just come from the township, they haven’t had water now for 11 days?

MADIBA: I am not aware that they haven’t had water for 11 days.

The municipality says in addition to looking into drilling more boreholes, they have thirty jojo tanks to distribute. We found some of these tanks in Maokeng – without water and wihtout taps.

And even with all the boreholes functioning, the water supply won’t be nearly enough, especially not for the town’s major industries.

SPASKI GELDENHUIS: A lot of businesses is dependable on water. You have the big abattoirs Country Meat and CC Chickens. Those people employ more than a 1000 people that’s just people working there. That’s not just the households.

David Niemann is Country Meat’s financial director.

DAVID NIEMANN: If we slaughter 275 units a day we use 275 thousand litres of water. We are in a fortunate position that we have alternatives, other possibilities that we can look at.

DEREK WHITFIELD: Country Meat and CC Chickens have been drilling on their own properties to find their own water supply. I believe that weighing up of life against the sustainability of business is going to come to the fore unfortunately very soon.

MORENA THEBE: The business of car wash will close down if no water.

And, the water shortage is creating another big problem.

DEREK WHITFIELD: And that is the sewerage. The town needs at least 4 million litres of water to be flushed down the sewers every day in order for it not to be blocked up.

THARINE HURTER: If you are a resident and you only have 20 litres of water, would you throw that in your toilet system or would you rather use it?

In times of crisis people stand together. This was evident in the human chain that formed within minutes after two trucks with donated water arranged by Water Shortage South Africa arrived in Kroonstad this week.

SPASKI GELDENHUIS: It doesn’t matter if you have money or not, you are going to bath out of buckets. It is really getting serious.





PROMO’S

PROMO 1: 15”

The third largest town in the Free State needs a miracle as taps start to run dry.

DEVI LINK: looking at it from up here, it is clear in my mind, Kroonstad is in trouble.

PROMO 2: 15”

DEV LINK: PROMO: The taps in Kroonstad have virtually run dry and with no rain predicted as we move into winter, this city needs a miracle.

SPASKI GELDENHUIS: It doesn’t matter if you have money or not, you are going to bath out of buckets. It is really getting serious.

PROMO 3: 10”

DEVI: Mama, how long you don’t have water here now?

CHRISTINA NCEDANE: One week and a half.

In less than three weeks, Kroonstad’s natural water supply will be depleted.

CHRIS DALTON: I would say 30% of blame should be on municipality for not making adequate plans, for not maintaining the existing water systems that we got, dams boreholes. For not implementing water restrictions timeously. The Municipal Manager, Mnce/disi Mq/wathi declined our request for an interview, saying it was “premature to talk about the matter.” But spokesperson Khojane Madiba eventually granted us an interview. KHOJANE MADIBA: We have put water restrictions in place. December, again, February, again May, we have now reduced the usuage of water – we are saying to people they must 15 kilolitres per month . DEVI: Why are we in this situation? KHOJANE MADIBA: We are in this situation Because there is no rain. DEVI: It is not just the rain. KHOJANE MADIBA: There is no water in the dams. DEVI: So you are blaming you completely on the drought? KHOJANE MADIBA: I don’t understand – are you saying we… DEVI: I am asking you, we have this situation in Kroonstad 100% because of the drought? KHOJANE MADIBA: Yes, it is as a result of the drought! DEVI: This is not just as a result of the drought? You have had failing infrastructure issues, lack of maintanence for year? KHOJANE MADIBA: The failing of infrastructure has contributed to the disaster? Is that what you are saying? DEVI: Yes, that is what I am saying! KHOJANE MADIBA: In any case, the problem with infrastructure in Kroonstad or in Moqhaka, we have got infrastructure that is old. And it has been there for years. People who constructed it, probably did not anticipate that the growth of the population is going to be too much. The municipal boreholes also haven’t been maintained over the years. DEREK WHITFIELD: The municipal boreholes that exist were drilled a long time ago for the drought in the early 90s, so their condition has deteriorated and they do need rejuvination. But the water from the boreholes that are operational will have to be treated before being consumed. DEREK WHITFIELD: Some of the boreholes are contaminated with e-coli, that is from sewer contamination. One of the boreholes in town is contaminated with hydro-carbon. One of the oil companies has been notified and they have taken samples. But it seems that contaminated tap water has been an issue in the past. Residents raised the alarm when water flowing from their taps looked like this - just three months ago. RESIDENT: I really don’t know what to say. The municipality said the water purification system is being upgraded to the tune of R39,2 million and will be completed in July. THARINE HURTER: Moqhaka Municipality only budgeted R56 million in the coming bookyear 2016/2017 for repairs and maintanence. R56 million out of R670 million budget is not enough. Residents are questioning the municipality’s lack of urgency to the water crisis. This water leaked from an open waste valve on the Suid/rand reservoir for six days this month. KHOJANA MADIBA: We agree that the leakages somehow creates to the problem of not having the water and we have been working very hard with out dedicated employees to close those leaks. We are satisfied now with the progress we have made. DEVI: I have just come from the township, they haven’t had water now for 11 days? MADIBA: I am not aware that they haven’t had water for 11 days. The municipality says in addition to looking into drilling more boreholes, they have thirty jojo tanks to distribute. We found some of these tanks in Maokeng – without water and wihtout taps. And even with all the boreholes functioning, the water supply won’t be nearly enough, especially not for the town’s major industries. SPASKI GELDENHUIS: A lot of businesses is dependable on water. You have the big abattoirs Country Meat and CC Chickens. Those people employ more than a 1000 people that’s just people working there. That’s not just the households. David Niemann is Country Meat’s financial director. DAVID NIEMANN: If we slaughter 275 units a day we use 275 thousand litres of water. We are in a fortunate position that we have alternatives, other possibilities that we can look at. DEREK WHITFIELD: Country Meat and CC Chickens have been drilling on their own properties to find their own water supply. I believe that weighing up of life against the sustainability of business is going to come to the fore unfortunately very soon. MORENA THEBE: The business of car wash will close down if no water. And, the water shortage is creating another big problem. DEREK WHITFIELD: And that is the sewerage. The town needs at least 4 million litres of water to be flushed down the sewers every day in order for it not to be blocked up. THARINE HURTER: If you are a resident and you only have 20 litres of water, would you throw that in your toilet system or would you rather use it? In times of crisis people stand together. This was evident in the human chain that formed within minutes after two trucks with donated water arranged by Water Shortage South Africa arrived in Kroonstad this week. SPASKI GELDENHUIS: It doesn’t matter if you have money or not, you are going to bath out of buckets. It is really getting serious. PROMO’S PROMO 1: 15” The third largest town in the Free State needs a miracle as taps start to run dry. DEVI LINK: looking at it from up here, it is clear in my mind, Kroonstad is in trouble. PROMO 2: 15” DEV LINK: PROMO: The taps in Kroonstad have virtually run dry and with no rain predicted as we move into winter, this city needs a miracle. SPASKI GELDENHUIS: It doesn’t matter if you have money or not, you are going to bath out of buckets. It is really getting serious. PROMO 3: 10” DEVI: Mama, how long you don’t have water here now? CHRISTINA NCEDANE: One week and a half. In less than three weeks, Kroonstad’s natural water supply will be depleted.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Kroonstad may be the first Free State town to run completely dry.The town's water reservoirs are on their last capacity and the False River from which they pump water to the town, almost dry.What then
metadata.Further information: KROONSTAD WATER SITUATION - Kroonstad Municipality sent out a notice two weeks ago that the town would have no water for three days this week (Wednesday to Friday) because of maintanence to one pump - The entire town is not without water, because there is still water left in the reservoir in town, but most parts of the town is without water - There is, however, greater concern over the water situation in Kroonstad: it could be the first town in the Free State to completely run dry and it could happen very soon: two to three weeks was an estimation given at a meeting last night - The town serves a population of about 150 000 (figure to be confirmed) - The Sterkfontein Dam is currently empty - The Groblersdam – that pumps water into the Bloemhof Dam – is nearly empty - The Bloemhof Dam is Kroonstad’s reservoir Dam and is currenly standing at 0,2% - The last dam that feeds water to Kroonstad is the Barend Wessels Dam – situated in the Vals River. Water to the town is currently being pumped to the town from this dam and it is at the lowest percentage it has ever been - Kroonstad uses 37 million litres of water per day - Even if ALL the boreholes in town are fully and a 100% operational, it will only provide 1 million litres of water WANTS KROONSTAD TO BE DECLARED DISASTER AREA - The Kroonstad Municipality is currently in a process with the Department of Water Affairs to have the town declared as a disaster area - Only when it has been declared as a disaster area, would the National Defence Force be able to help with the drilling of extra boreholes or supplying water to residents in town if the town runs dry - Supplying water with water tankers alone, would not be efficient to supply water to all the residents in town CONSEQUENCES FOR BIG BUSINESSES - Kroonstad has a few huge industries in town. These include: - ** Sasko – not as big as it once was – but still a business that uses a lot of water - ** Premier Milling – wheat and maize mills - ** CC Chicken – supplies chicken countrywide and employs 600 workers – they have recently sunked 6 boreholes, but say it will still not provide them with enough water and if the town runs dry, they will have to close the business and let the workers go until there is water again - ** Country Meat & Fernick Abbatoir – they have recently sunked 4 boreholes and they are also concerned that these 4 boreholes will not provide enough water for them to continue with their business as they currently do. They provide meat countrywide
